(1) disorder is a necessary ingredient for the suppression of $T_c$, (2) boson fluctuations dominate in wide wires, while fermion ones are important in narrow ones, and (3) in the presence of disorder bosons are always important.
the interplay between Coulomb repulsion and disorder is responsible for the destruction of super-conductivity in quasi-one dimensional wires.

In summary, our research is concerned with

the study of a number of fundamental problems in condensed matter physics and quantum field theory: (1) the interplay between the Coulomb repulsion, disorder, and quantum fluctuations in quasi-one dimensional systems; (2) the interplay of disorder and Coulomb interaction in the theory of the quantum Hall effect and its generalizations.
the interplay between Coulomb interaction, disorder and dimensionality.
the study of the interplay between fermionic and boson mechanisms of suppression of the superconducting transition temperature $T_c$.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the suppression of superconducting order is a complex interplay between the mean field $T_c$ reduction and fluctuations.
in a disordered wire with Coulomb repulsion, the mean field critical $T_c$ is reduced by fermionic mechanisms, and the superconductivity is destroyed by bosonic mechanisms at a lower temperature.
the suppression of superconducting order in disordered quasi-one-dimensional systems is determined by both fermionic and quantum bosonic fluctuations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the boson mechanism of superconductivity suppression is the dominant one for the case of narrow wires and weak disorder, while the fermion mechanism is dominant for the case of wide wires and strong disorder.
the bosonic suppression is the dominant one in the regime where $T_c$ is low.
in narrow wires the bosonic suppression dominates, while in wide wires the fermionic mechanism is more relevant.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the interplay between fermionic and boson mechanisms can lead to a variety of behaviors in amorphous wires.
the interplay between the fermionic and boson mechanisms is responsible for the nonmonotonic behavior in the superconducting critical temperature $T_s$ as a function of disorder strength.
the interplay of disorder and Coulomb interactions leads to the suppression of superconducting order parameter and the appearance of a pseudogap in the density of states.
